proposals.name: 99 Kingdoms
proposals.type: War-torn nations of the Sayir Sea
proposals.entry:
The 99 Kingdoms are the named nations, city-states, sea-powers, and displaced polities drawn into the formal War of the 99 Kingdoms, usually called the 99 War. The number is a political name, not a census: far more than ninety-nine states, peoples, and newly found territories are involved. Fogport is not one of them. It remains the war’s only neutral city-state because every side still needs its harbor, markets, messengers, and somewhere dangerous to meet.

The Four Great Powers

Veyr, the Gravoska Kingdom, the Devor Ascendancy, and Mung are the four powers capable of changing the whole shape of the war. They are not allies. Each embodies a different answer to what a nation is for: refinement and custody; law and mass industry; collective consumption; or sheer replaceable manpower.

Devor is the state. The Thrx are its insectile people and hive intelligence. A Thrx ambassador may wear velvet and speak of an Emperor; the hive behind it values living beings as industrial resources.

Known Nations and Powers

  • Veyr: A great sea-facing republic of tall, fine-boned people, canal cities, clock-priests, mathematicians, funeral machinists, true Apparatus, and roughly twenty-foot Battle Matons. Its immaculate design culture treats dangerous knowledge as a civic burden, not private property.
  • The Gravoska Kingdom (Gravosk): A northern great power of thick-built people, compulsory service, rugged ships, foundries, artillery, and law older than its crown. Foreigners call it Gravosk; its First Witness commands a nation already trained to report for war.
  • The Devor Ascendancy: A great imperial hive-state of the insectile Thrx. Devor treats forests, animals, and captured peoples as fuel and inventory; its courtly Emperor is an interface for a collective intelligence, not its ruler.
  • Mung: A fourth great power built on extreme manpower: compact blue-gray humanoids bred and trained for relentless mobilization, armed with stout spring weapons and natural teeth. Mung has little private culture beyond function, reproduction, and conquest—and covets the strange freedoms of other peoples.
  • Serevane: A crowded river kingdom of blockade survivors whose relief houses, laundries, and medical caravans form one of the war’s best spy-and-smuggler networks.
  • Odrava: An ingenious manufacturing state whose workshops compete to make engines smaller, stranger, and more capable than sensible people need; it sells to every side while its devices acquire unnerving habits.
  • Ulmar: A cold maritime kingdom of storm-watchers, whale oil, cliff harbors, and sea-law. Its navigators insist the Sayir Sea holds grudges, and their predictions about Fogport are becoming inconveniently accurate.
  • Keth: A theatrical monarchy where diplomacy, legal testimony, mourning, espionage, and public performance are indistinguishable.
  • Hask: A hard coast of wreckers, salvagers, and tide-fortresses, where a dead ship is public salvage if no one asks too closely about the crew.
  • Bellor: A devotional kingdom of roadside shrines, saint-bearers, traveling healers, keys, relics, and strict hospitality; its portable sanctuaries often conceal prisoner extraction or relic theft.
  • Orsava: An urban kingdom where contracts are sacred, swordsmanship fashionable, and even an insult may require witnesses and paperwork.
  • Ravel: A patchwork of floodplains, old roads, messenger monasteries, and stubborn towns with the finest courier network in the known world.
  • Merroway: A misty coast that believes an unmourned accidental death leaves a dangerous hole in the world; its armies bring singers and memorial clerks to war.
  • Drom: A mercantile city-kingdom that buys ruined ports, condemned districts, debt-ridden fortresses, and future favors wherever war leaves a crack.
  • Kadovar — The Funeral Republic: A nation of the dead, still populated by those killed in the Pale Weather three centuries ago. Its mortuary surgeons and Retrieval Companies fight because no new Kadovarians can ever be born.
  • Orlania: A destroyed iron-island nation of sailors, smiths, mercenaries, tusked people, and blue-black tattoos. Its survivors dispute whether their homeland is dead or merely occupied.
  • Trovus: The power that broke Orlania after it refused military access to its harbors. Its wider character remains deliberately unfinished; its crime against Orlania is not.
  • Ors Varkesh: The partitioned homeland of the Varkesh: an industrial wetland kingdom of foundries, canals, fortified farms, masks, oaths, and skilled labor, now occupied in all but name.
  • Pellinor: A paper-and-lock republic where citizenship exists only while records do. Its legally erased exiles hire Fogport smugglers to steal back their names.
  • Sablemark: Black-stone islands whose noble houses breed giant seabirds for mail, scouting, and naval sabotage.
  • The Kharad Marches: Fortified farming towns where every household keeps an arsenal and votes only after public wrestling matches; their grain trains feed armies and invite raids.
  • Vesca: A stilted lake kingdom above drowned ruins, exporting pearl-glass and divers who can reach what other nations sealed underwater.
  • Aderra: A mountain confederacy that elects rulers by debt auction: the person willing to assume the greatest public obligation governs.
  • Caldress: A wine country whose surgeons discovered certain vintages preserve memory in blood; every power wants its vineyards.
  • Yarrow: A wetland monarchy where judges travel by barge and borders move whenever the river does.
  • Tern: A lighthouse coast whose rescue crews have saved everyone’s sailors and therefore know whose navies sink their own ships.
  • Hollis: Quarry cities inside a single great ravine, selling stonework, prison labor, and siege engineers; miners have broken into something inhabited.
  • Salmora: A salt kingdom where preservation is morally suspect and smugglers move salt, bodies, and relics through the same routes.
  • Eldrake: A forest republic whose soldiers fight with sworn witnesses; someone is murdering witnesses in Fogport to erase victories.
  • The Seven Cantons of Brin: Seven alpine states joined by one rail tunnel and mutual defense, each having sold access rights to a different belligerent.
  • Myr: An arid scholarly kingdom that grows medicine fungi in tombs; its grave-gardens contain people who may have been buried too early.
  • The Red Tesselate: City-states whose borders are tiled roads rather than terrain; changing road signs can conquer a village without entering it.
  • Nocera: A naval republic in which each ship’s crew is legally family; captains will sacrifice aristocrats before abandoning deckhands.
  • Karst: Cave monasteries that train combat medics, mountaineers, and professional survivors; their evacuation routes now move weapons.
  • Ivenza: A kingdom of mirror-makers and theatrical architects, built to confuse invaders; its capital is partly fake.
  • The Oltan Freeholds: Former imperial estates governed by repair guilds, militias, and armed village councils—free, messy, and coveted.
  • Barras: A coastal maker of locks, safes, prison doors, and escape artists; its diplomatic gift is a key that opens nothing until it must.
  • Neme: An agricultural kingdom raising huge work-beasts for plows and siege guns; the beasts have begun refusing certain officers.
  • Rusk: A cold republic of ice roads and brutal election festivals; spring exposes battlefields whose dead appear to have changed sides.
  • Chyron: A delta society where people inherit occupations rather than surnames; its navigators sabotage floodworks to hide a dynastic fraud.
  • Vallach: A nation of traveling fairs, machine shows, and patent duels, where every invention must be publicly demonstrated.
  • Esh: A desert pilgrimage state whose armed well-trusts control water routes needed by southern armies.
  • The Braid Isles: Low islands united by marriage treaties, tidal calendars, and cutters that can make fleets vanish into safe water.
  • Mournhold: An upland state that pays widows directly and counts every casualty correctly; its clerks are hunted across the war.
  • Civara: A federation of enormous public kitchens; its ration ledgers are the best espionage archive on the continent.
  • Thornwake: A rain-soaked border kingdom growing living hedges into roads, walls, and ambushes; its forests are hungry for soldiers.
  • Dask: A former garrison state that won freedom by stealing payroll, artillery manuals, and officers’ families—excellent at rebellion, terrible at peace.

Only a fraction of the participants in the 99 War are known in detail. Every Fogport ship, refugee family, crate, embassy, borrowed uniform, and debt may introduce another.
